metadata.title: Chapter 10: The Sermon at Benares (First Flight)
metadata.subtitle: Interactive Full-Text Reading & Board Mastery
metadata.subject: English
metadata.author: Antigravity Supreme Intelligence
learning_outcomes: Read and comprehend the original NCERT First Flight text without omissions.
Understand the core Buddhist philosophy regarding the inevitability of death and the futility of lamentation.
Master difficult archaic and formal vocabulary with contextual bilingual translations.
Analyze the profound character transformation of Kisa Gotami.
Prepare high-scoring answers for Board Exam RTCs (Reference to Context) and Long Answer Questions.

ai_context.learning_goal: Provide the complete, unabridged NCERT text broken into logical thematic passages with bilingual inline translations and Socratic pedagogy.
common_misconceptions: Students often believe Buddha was being cold-hearted by asking for mustard seeds, failing to see that experiential learning was the only cure for her blind grief.
Students confuse 'immortality' in the text as physical eternal life, whereas Buddha refers to spiritual liberation from the cycle of suffering.

blocks.content:
Have you ever experienced a loss so profound that your mind refused to accept reality? When Kisa Gotami lost her only child, she wandered the streets asking for medicine to revive a lifeless body.

How does Gautama Buddha `(गौतम बुद्ध / ગૌતમ બુદ્ધ)` guide a grieving mother from blinding despair to universal enlightenment without giving a dry lecture?

Let's read the *complete, original text* of this timeless chapter to understand the most profound sermon ever preached on mortality `(मरणशीलता / નશ્વરતા)`.
Gautama Buddha preaching his first sermon at the holy city of Benares to his disciples.
blocks.alt_text: Lord Buddha delivering a sermon under a tree near the holy river Ganges in Benares.

blocks.title: Passage 1: The Prince and the Sights of Suffering
blocks.content:
Gautama Buddha (563 B.C. – 483 B.C.) began life as a prince named Siddhartha Gautama, in northern India. At twelve, he was sent away for schooling in the Hindu sacred scriptures `(पवित्र धर्मग्रंथ / પવિત્ર ધર્મગ્રંથો)` and four years later he returned home to marry a princess. They had a son and lived for ten years as befitted royalty `(राजसी ठाठ-बाट / રાજવી ઠાઠમાઠ)`.

At about the age of twenty-five, the Prince, heretofore shielded `(अब तक सुरक्षित / અત્યાર સુધી સુરક્ષિત)` from the sufferings of the world, while out hunting chanced upon `(अचानक देखा / અચાનક જોયું)` a sick man, then an aged man, then a funeral procession `(शवयात्रा / સ્મશાનયાત્રા)`, and finally a monk `(संन्यासी / સાધુ)` begging for alms `(भिक्षा / ભિક્ષા)`.

These sights so moved him that he at once went out into the world to seek enlightenment `(आत्मज्ञान या बोध / આત્મજ્ઞાન કે બોધ)` concerning the sorrows he had witnessed.

💡 **Teacher's Insight (The Four Great Sights):** Notice the dramatic turning point in Prince Siddhartha's life at age 25. He witnessed four distinct sights:
1. A sick man (Physical pain)
2. An aged man (Decay of youth)
3. A funeral procession (Inevitability of death)
4. An ascetic/monk begging for alms (The search for truth and liberation)
These four sights shattered his royal bubble and compelled him to renounce all worldly pleasures.

content.question: At what age was Siddhartha Gautama sent away for schooling, and when did he witness the four sights of suffering?
options: Sent away at age 10, witnessed sights at age 20
Sent away at age 12, witnessed sights at age 25
Sent away at age 16, witnessed sights at age 30
Sent away at age 14, witnessed sights at age 28
content.correct_answer: Sent away at age 12, witnessed sights at age 25
content.explanation: According to the NCERT text, he was sent for schooling in sacred scriptures at age 12, returned at 16 to marry, and at about age 25 chanced upon the four sights of suffering.

blocks.title: Passage 2: The Enlightenment and the First Sermon
blocks.content:
He wandered for seven years and finally sat down under a peepal tree `(पीपल का पेड़ / પીપળાનું વૃક્ષ)`, where he vowed `(शपथ ली / પ્રતિજ્ઞા લીધી)` to stay until enlightenment came. Enlightened after seven days, he renamed the tree the Bodhi Tree (Tree of Wisdom) and began to teach and to share his new understandings. At that point he became known as the Buddha (the Awakened or the Enlightened `(प्रबुद्ध / જાગૃત)`).

The Buddha preached `(उपदेश दिया / ઉપદેશ આપ્યો)` his first sermon `(धार्मिक उपदेश / ધાર્મિક પ્રવચન)` at the city of Benares, most holy of the dipping places `(पवित्र स्नान स्थल / પવિત્ર સ્નાન સ્થળ)` on the River Ganges. That sermon has been preserved and is given here. It reflects the Buddha's wisdom about one inscrutable `(रहस्यमय या समझ से परे / ગૂઢ કે અગમ્ય)` kind of suffering.

🔥 **Board Exam Significance:** Why did Buddha choose Benares (Varanasi) for his first sermon?
Benares is regarded as the holiest city on the banks of the Ganges where millions seek spiritual cleansing. Choosing Benares symbolized that his teachings were intended to purify humanity from the deepest, most 'inscrutable' kind of grief—the fear and sorrow of death.

blocks.title: Passage 3: Kisa Gotami's Grief and Desperation
blocks.content:
Kisa Gotami had an only son, and he died. In her grief `(गहरा शोक / ઊંડો શોક)` she carried the dead child to all her neighbours, asking them for medicine, and the people said, "She has lost her senses `(अपनी सुध-बुध खो बैठी है / ભાન ભૂલી ગઈ છે)`. The boy is dead."

At length `(काफ़ी समय बाद / આખરે)`, Kisa Gotami met a man who replied to her request, "I cannot give thee medicine for thy child, but I know a physician `(वैद्य या चिकित्सक / વૈદ્ય કે તબીબ)` who can."

And the girl said, "Pray tell me, sir; who is it?"

And the man replied, "Go to Sakyamuni `(शाक्यमुनि / શાક્યમુનિ)`, the Buddha."

content.question: Why did people say that Kisa Gotami had 'lost her senses'?
options: Because she gave all her wealth to strangers
Because she carried her dead son to neighbours asking for medicine
Because she refused to marry again
Because she ran into the forest alone
content.correct_answer: Because she carried her dead son to neighbours asking for medicine
content.explanation: Her motherly grief was so immense that she refused to accept the finality of death, wandering everywhere with her dead child asking for medicine to revive him.

blocks.title: Passage 4: The Condition of the Mustard Seed
blocks.content:
Kisa Gotami repaired `(गई / ગઈ)` to the Buddha and cried, "Lord and Master, give me the medicine that will cure my boy."

The Buddha answered, "I want a handful of mustard-seed `(सरसों के बीज / રાઈના દાણા)`."

And when the girl in her joy promised to procure `(प्राप्त करना या लाना / મેળવવું)` it, the Buddha added, "The mustard-seed must be taken from a house where no son, daughter, father or mother has died."

💡 **Pedagogical Brilliance of the Buddha:**
Notice Buddha's pedagogical method! He did not engage in philosophical debate or tell her bluntly that the dead cannot return. Instead, he gave her an active task. Mustard seeds were cheap and available in every Indian household, giving her instant hope—yet the condition attached held the universal truth.

blocks.title: Passage 5: The Fruitless Search
blocks.content:
Poor Kisa Gotami now went from house to house, and the people pitied her and said, "Here is mustard-seed; take it!"

But when she asked, "Did a son or daughter, a father or mother, die in your family?" they answered her, "Alas! `(हाय! / અરેરે!)` the living are few, but the dead are many. Do not remind us of our deepest grief."

And there was no house but some beloved one had died in it.

content.question: What did the people reply when Kisa Gotami asked if anyone had died in their family?
options: "We have plenty of medicine for your child."
"The living are few, but the dead are many."
"Only the elderly die in our village."
"No one has ever passed away in this house."
content.correct_answer: "The living are few, but the dead are many."
content.explanation: Every household reminded her of their lost beloved ones, emphasizing that death has touched every single family across humanity.

blocks.content: Kisa Gotami sitting weary by the roadside, gazing at the flickering city lights fading into darkness.
blocks.alt_text: A tired woman sitting on the outskirts of the city at twilight, watching the city lamps flicker and extinguish.

blocks.title: Passage 6: Awakening by the Wayside (The Flickering Lights)
blocks.content:
Kisa Gotami became weary `(थक कर चूर / ખૂબ થાકેલી)` and hopeless, and sat down at the wayside watching the lights of the city, as they flickered up `(टिमटिमाईं / ઝબૂકી)` and were extinguished again `(बुझ गईं / ઓલવાઈ ગઈ)`. At last the darkness of the night reigned everywhere `(चारों ओर छा गई / ચારેય તરફ છવાઈ ગઈ)`.

And she considered the fate of men, that their lives flicker up and are extinguished again. And she thought to herself, "How selfish am I in my grief! Death is common to all `(मृत्यु सभी के लिए समान है / મૃત્યુ સૌ માટે સમાન છે)`; yet in this valley of desolation `(शोक और घोर निराशा की घाटी / દુઃખ અને વેરાન ખીણ)` there is a path that leads him to immortality `(अमरता / અમરત્વ)` who has surrendered all selfishness `(समस्त स्वार्थ त्याग दिया हो / સમગ્ર સ્વાર્થ ત્યજી દીધો હોય)`."

🔥 **Symbolism & Literary Analysis (The Flickering Lights):**
- **City lights flickering and extinguishing:** A metaphor for human lives—sparkling briefly and eventually getting snuffed out by death.
- **Selfishness:** Kisa Gotami realizes her grief was selfish because she thought only her child had died, ignoring the universal pain of all mankind.
- **Valley of Desolation:** Represents the worldly life full of sorrow and loss.
- **Immortality:** Does not mean physical immortality of the body, but spiritual liberation (Nirvana) attained by overcoming selfish attachment.

content.question: What profound realization dawned upon Kisa Gotami as she watched the city lights flicker and extinguish?
options: That she needed to travel to another town for mustard seeds
That human lives flicker up and extinguish just like the lights, and death is common to all
That the Buddha had deceived her with an impossible condition
That she should build a memorial for her son in Benares
content.correct_answer: That human lives flicker up and extinguish just like the lights, and death is common to all
content.explanation: Watching the city lights fade into the darkness of the night, she realized that mortal existence is brief and fragile, and that her individual grief was part of a universal human reality.

blocks.title: Passage 7: The Nature of Mortals and Earthen Vessels
blocks.content:
The Buddha said: "The life of mortals `(मरणशील प्राणी / નશ્વર જીવો)` in this world is troubled and brief and combined with pain. For there is not any means by which those that have been born can avoid dying; after reaching old age there is death; of such a nature are living beings.

As ripe fruits are early in danger of falling, so mortals when born are always in danger of death. As all earthen vessels `(मिट्टी के बर्तन / માટીનાં વાસણો)` made by the potter end in being broken, so is the life of mortals. Both young and adult, both those who are fools and those who are wise, all fall into the power of death; all are subject to death `(मृत्यु के अधीन / મૃત્યુને આધીન)`."

💡 **Mastering Analogies in the Sermon:**
Buddha uses two striking analogies in this passage:
1. **Ripe Fruits:** Just as a ripe fruit is constantly in danger of falling from the branch, every living human is in constant danger of death from the moment of birth.
2. **Earthen Pots made by a Potter:** Regardless of their size, shape, or beauty, every earthen vessel will eventually break. Similarly, both fools and the wise, rich and poor, inevitably meet death.

blocks.title: Passage 8: The Arrow of Lamentation and Peace of Mind
blocks.content:
"Of those who, overcome by death, depart from life, a father cannot save his son, nor kinsmen `(सगे-संबंधी / સગાંવહાલાં)` their relations. Mark! `(ध्यान दें! / ધ્યાન આપો!)` while relatives are looking on and lamenting `(विलाप करते हुए / વિલાપ કરતાં કરતાં)` deeply, one by one mortals are carried off, like an ox that is led to the slaughter `(कसाईखाना / કતલખાનું)`.

So the world is afflicted `(पीड़ाग्रस्त / પીડિત)` with death and decay, therefore the wise do not grieve `(शोक मनाना / શોક કરવો)`, knowing the terms of the world.

Not from weeping nor from grieving will anyone obtain peace of mind; on the contrary, his pain will be the greater and his body will suffer. He will make himself sick and pale, yet the dead are not saved by his lamentation `(विलाप / રુદન કે વિલાપ)`. He who seeks peace should draw out the arrow of lamentation, and complaint, and grief. He who has drawn out the arrow and has become composed `(शांत और स्थिरचित्त / શાંત અને સ્વસ્થ)` will obtain peace of mind; he who has overcome all sorrow will become free from sorrow, and be blessed `(धन्य / ધન્ય)`."

content.question: According to Gautama Buddha, what happens to a person who continues to weep and grieve excessively?
options: Their departed loved ones are brought back to life
Their pain becomes greater, their body suffers, and they make themselves sick and pale without saving the dead
They achieve instant enlightenment and spiritual peace
The gods take pity on them and grant them immortality
content.correct_answer: Their pain becomes greater, their body suffers, and they make themselves sick and pale without saving the dead
content.explanation: Buddha explicitly states that weeping and lamentation cannot save the dead; it only multiplies physical and emotional suffering. Peace comes only when one draws out the arrow of grief.

blocks.content:
🔥 **BOARD EXAM SPECIAL: MASTER QUESTION & ANSWER BLUEPRINT**

**Q1. How did Buddha make Kisa Gotami understand the universal truth of life and death?**
*Model Answer:* Instead of giving a theoretical lecture, Buddha employed an experiential method. He asked Kisa Gotami to bring a handful of mustard seeds from a house where no loved one had ever died. As she went door-to-door, she discovered that every household had lost a father, mother, child, or kinsman. Watching the flickering city lights at dusk, she realized that human life is transient and death is common to all mortals. Thus, she overcame her selfish grief.

**Q2. What is the significance of the 'Arrow of Lamentation'?**
*Model Answer:* Lamentation, sorrow, and endless complaints are compared to a poisonous arrow stuck in the heart. As long as the arrow remains, it causes deep anguish and physically sickens the body without bringing the dead back. One who pulls out this arrow through acceptance and wisdom becomes calm, composed, and blessed with true peace of mind.

**Key Vocabulary for 5-Mark Answers:**
- **Inscrutable:** Incapable of being understood.
- **Lamentation:** Passionate expression of grief.
- **Mortals:** Living beings destined to die.
- **Afflicted:** Burdened with pain or distress.
- **Composed:** Calm, tranquil, and self-possessed.
